This study introduces a nonparametric test for regression functions that does not rely on any structural constraints, such as linearity or monotonicity. The approach is grounded in a novel, data-driven kernel selection method. We demonstrate that, under a local alternative hypothesis, the test's asymptotic power is derived from a specific, well-defined asymptotic power function. Additionally, we establish the consistency of a data-driven bandwidth selector. To validate our methodology, we employ both simulation experiments and a real-world case study.

This study investigates the efficacy of multilingual models versus unilingual models for analyzing social media content. We evaluate the performance of a range of unilingual and multilingual architectures across various tasks, including text classification, keyword generation, and multilingual sentiment analysis. Our findings indicate that multilingual models achieve comparable performance to unilingual models, with the exception of language-specific tasks. Additionally, we examine the impact of data augmentation and the use of language embeddings on model outcomes.

Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is a widely used neuroimaging technique for diagnosing and monitoring brain disorders. While deep learning has recently been applied to brain image analysis, the specific advantages of these architectures in classifying brain states remain unclear. This study evaluates the performance of various deep learning models using fMRI data from the ADHD-200 dataset, which includes resting-state scans from 500 participants diagnosed with ADHD, along with 500 healthy controls. We compare the efficacy of several architectures, including 1D-CNN, 2D-CNN, LSTM, GRU, and a novel 3D-CNN, to determine their suitability for this task. Our findings indicate that the 3D-CNN architecture achieves the highest accuracy in classifying brain disorders, attaining 94.1% on the validation set and 93.1% on the test set. Furthermore, the model demonstrates superior generalization, attaining 89.1% accuracy on an external test set.

This study examines the convergence rate of the linear quadratic regulator (LQR) for time-varying linear systems. We demonstrate that the rate at which the state feedback gain matrix converges is fundamentally determined by the energy dissipation characteristics of the associated closed-loop system. Specifically, if the closed-loop system exhibits exponential stability, the convergence of the LQR state feedback gain matrix occurs at an exponential rate.

This study introduces a boundary treatment approach for high-order numerical schemes that integrates the characteristics of high-order interior points with first-order boundary conditions. By utilizing the boundary conditions to reconstruct the solution at the grid point immediately adjacent to the boundary, the method ensures that the overall accuracy matches that of the interior scheme. The proposed technique is demonstrated to be stable, straightforward to implement, and capable of handling complex scenarios such as curved boundaries and multi-dimensional problems.

We present a theoretical analysis of a silicon film on silicon dioxide, paired with a photonic crystal back reflector (PCBR) made of silicon. This configuration is designed to achieve high optical absorption in ultra-thin films, a requirement for future photovoltaic technologies. Our results indicate that the PCBR significantly enhances absorption in thin films by trapping light within the silicon layer. Specifically, a silicon film measuring 100 nm in thickness can reach 90% absorption when paired with an optimal 300 nm thick PCBR. This performance is achieved by tailoring the PCBR's band structure to create a photonic bandgap that aligns with the silicon film's optical resonances.

Valuation algebra serves as a powerful framework for representing and computing with uncertainty. This paper extends that framework to credal sets, which are collections of probability distributions. We establish that fundamental operations—specifically combination, marginalization, and revision—are well-defined for credal sets, and we provide efficient algorithms for executing these tasks. This extension enables the application of valuation algebra to handle uncertainty modeled by sets of probability distributions. We demonstrate the utility of this approach through a case study on Bayesian network revision, outlining both its formal semantics and computational methods.

We introduce a distance-based recommendation model that utilizes the Wasserstein distance to measure the discrepancy between a user's preference distribution and the item distribution. The primary advantage of this approach is that it does not require the explicit extraction of a user's preference vector, thereby eliminating the need for a separate learning phase. Instead, the model directly utilizes the item distribution to calculate the Wasserstein distance, enabling immediate generation of recommendations without any training process. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this distance-based method can be derived from a probabilistic framework, which establishes a theoretical link between distance and learning-to-rank. Finally, our experimental results indicate that this approach achieves performance comparable to traditional learning-to-rank models.

This study introduces a generalization of the widely recognized amplitude-damping channel, termed the quasi-ENMM GAD channel, which exhibits non-Markovian dynamics for any parameter value. Unlike previous models that display non-Markovian characteristics only within specific parameter ranges, this proposed channel retains its non-Markovian nature universally. The analysis further examines the impact of this non-Markovian behavior on the system's evolution, specifically addressing the reduction in state purity and the mitigation of information loss. Additionally, the work details how to synthesize the quasi-ENMM GAD channel using auxiliary systems and elementary quantum channels, while also deriving the corresponding quantum relative entropy of non-Markovity for this channel.

This study introduces Contrastive Contrastive Augmentation for Real-World Images (CCRAL), a novel technique designed to enhance model generalization for unseen data. The method operates by first generating augmented versions of training images and then deriving a second augmented version from the initial one. The model is trained to minimize the distance between representations of the doubly-augmented image and the original once-augmented image while simultaneously maximizing the distance between them. By aligning the feature space of doubly-augmented images closer to that of singly-augmented images, CCRAL enables models to learn more robust and generalized features. Empirical evaluations on the ImageNet benchmark demonstrate that CCRAL achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

Creating semantic maps is crucial for enabling robots to perform tasks autonomously, yet the process is laborious and prone to errors. This paper introduces a new approach to automatically assign semantic labels to 2D grid maps by utilizing a pre-trained, open-domain language model. The proposed method, Semantic Concept Activation (SCA), operates by identifying semantically relevant terms within the robot's navigation logs and assessing their activation levels across various areas of the surrounding environment. SCA effectively integrates semantic knowledge from the language model with the robot's specific experiences, thereby generating meaningful and context-aware maps. Experimental results demonstrate that SCA surpasses existing methods in both accuracy and generalization capabilities. Furthermore, the framework is adaptable to other data sources, such as sensor imagery, and can be extended to support more complex semantic concepts.

This paper introduces Rikudo, a logic-based logic puzzle recently featured in the New York Times. The objective is to determine the connections between nodes in a graph such that every node connects to exactly two others, ensuring no cycles are formed. We establish that if all numbers within the grid are odd, the puzzle can be solved efficiently in polynomial time. Conversely, for any $\epsilon > 0$, determining solvability within $O(n^\epsilon)$ time is impossible for instances containing an exponential number of odd entries.

This study introduces a novel algorithm designed to address the computational challenges of solving large-scale linear programs (LPs) that arise in learning-to-optimize frameworks. The core approach involves reformulating the LP as a constrained optimization problem, which is then solved using the Sinkhorn algorithm. This method leverages the exponential convergence of the latter to achieve a significant reduction in computational complexity. The proposed method is validated through its application to the learning-to-optimize task of determining the optimal control policy for a linear quadratic regulator. The findings demonstrate that the algorithm achieves a substantial decrease in both computational time and memory usage, making it particularly effective for large-scale LPs.

This paper investigates the generalized modular equation and the associated polynomial $P(\lambda, \mu)=0$, which are linked by the relationship that any pair of solutions $(\lambda, \mu)$ must satisfy this connection. The work demonstrates that the degree of the generalized modular equation corresponds to the degree of the polynomial $P(\lambda, \mu)=0$, and it establishes that the pair $(\lambda, \mu)$ constitutes the set of all roots for the equation $P(\lambda, \mu)=0$.

We report the detection of a gravitational lens system, J0818-2613, which exhibits a quasar image configuration consistent with a single background quasar being bent by a foreground galaxy. The redshifts of the deflector and the deflected source are $z=0.41$ and $z=0.72$, respectively. This system is notable for its high redshifts, with the deflector ranking as the third most distant one identified to date. The lensing geometry is characterized by a single quasar image, a rarity among high-redshift systems. The observed flux of the image is approximately 10% of the flux from the unlensed counterpart. This study addresses a class of initial value problems associated with $q$-difference equations defined by $\frac{d}{d q} y(t)=\lambda y(t)+f(t)$, where the operator is given as $\frac{d}{d q} y(t)=\frac{y(t)-q y(q t)}{t}$. The analysis demonstrates that the $q$-exponential function serves as the fundamental solution to this operator. Furthermore, utilizing the difference method, it is established that the Cauchy problem for the $q$-difference equation $f\frac{d}{d q} y(t)=\lambda y(t)+f(t)$ admits the unique solution $y(t)=f(t)+\frac{1}{t}\int_{0}^{t} \frac{d}{d q} f(s)\exp \left(\frac{\lambda}{1-q}\left(t-s\right)\right) d s$.

This study investigates the phonon Hall effect (PHE) in dielectric materials, focusing on the impact of an applied magnetic field on phonon Hall conductivity ($\kappa_{xy}$). We demonstrate that $\kappa_{xy}$ is governed by the magnetic field's modulation of phonon group velocities and drift angles. Furthermore, we analyze the relationship between $\kappa_{xy}$ and the magnetic field strength, revealing that $\kappa_{xy}$ can be enhanced by increasing the magnetic field. Additionally, we identify that $\kappa_{xy}$ is sensitive to the material's dielectric properties, with the magnitude of $\kappa_{xy}$ varying based on the specific dielectric characteristics of the material.

Wide-field imaging systems are increasingly utilized in astronomy, particularly for ground-based optical and infrared observations. However, these setups face challenges in achieving high spatial resolution and managing light loss caused by field stops. This paper introduces a new nod and shuffle method designed to enhance both resolution and sensitivity. The technique involves splitting the field into two halves, which are sequentially imaged at distinct locations on the detector. This approach allows for the rejection of background noise and the rejection of skyglow, while simultaneously reducing acquisition times. The authors demonstrate the method's efficacy through simulations and observations conducted with the 1.5-meter telescope at the University of Hawaii's 2.2-meter telescope. The results indicate that the nod and shuffle technique can achieve a 20% improvement in spatial resolution and a 25% improvement in sensitivity.

This study establishes novel inequalities regarding the matrix logarithm, matrix exponentials, and commutators, extending the work of H. F. Smollarsky. We establish these inequalities in both integral and functional forms. By employing matrix versions of the Jensen, Hardy, and Minkowski inequalities, we derive rigorous proofs. These results hold for both Hermitian and positive definite matrices.

This study examines the behavior of the averaged null energy condition (ANEC) within the spherously symmetric black hole model proposed by s and Soleng. We find that the null energy average is violated during the black hole's formation phase and remains so throughout its evaporation.

In a four-dimensional Conformal Field Theory (CFT), the trace anomaly is characterized by three conformal field theory (CFT) parameters: $a$, $c$, and $k$. This study examines how these coefficients change when a relevant operator with integer conformal dimension is added to the theory. We demonstrate that the resulting theory exhibits a linear scaling of $a$, $c$, and $k$ with respect to the number of such operators. This linear behavior persists even in the limit of an infinite number of operators, provided the scaling dimension of the added operators remains an integer. Furthermore, we establish that the scaling dimensions of the squared stress tensor operator and mixed correlators involving the trace anomaly and the added operators are likewise linear in this limit. These findings are corroborated by calculations within free theories.

This paper introduces a maturity model for analyzing Internet of Things (IoT) testbeds, specifically focusing on Cyber-Physical Systems (ICS). The model's development utilizes a comparative analysis of existing models, which led to the identification of key criteria for evaluating ICS testbed maturity. The resulting framework is designed to foster continuous improvement within these environments. The model's validity was confirmed through its application to two real-world ICS testbeds, demonstrating its effectiveness.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has garnered significant attention in recent years, with numerous algorithms developed to address diverse applications. However, the majority of existing approaches rely on centralized training and decentralized execution, which often struggle to scale effectively in environments with high-dimensional observations and large agent counts. This paper introduces a new MARL algorithm grounded in greedy-based value representation (GVR). The GVR framework enables agents to learn a greedy policy that maximizes the value of a state-action pair, utilizing a hierarchical structure to capture both individual and joint state values. This design allows the system to efficiently process high-dimensional inputs. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the GVR approach can achieve an optimal policy within a finite number of steps. Empirical evaluations across various MARL benchmarks, including the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC) and the game of Go, reveal that the proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques.

We introduce SteroSet, a dataset designed to assess stereotypical biases across gender and racial categories within four distinct domains: occupation, adjective descriptions, activities, and media. This collection comprises 50,000 word pairs, with each pair consisting of two terms from different social groups (e.g., different genders or races) within the same domain. This structure enables the evaluation of stereotypical associations between specific social groups and those of other groups. To facilitate this, we developed a new metric that quantifies the probability of two word pairs occurring together based on their co-occurrence in extensive corpora. We evaluated numerous datasets using this new metric and found that existing methods, including Word2vec GloVe, and DeBias, exhibit significant stereotypical biases across all domains. Additionally, we introduced a novel dataset, "Stereosett," which is publicly available for further research.

This study introduces a new network optimization framework that integrates the Contextual Multi-Armed-Bandit (CMAB) approach with a deep neural network (DNN) to create a data-driven method for optimizing network tilt. In this CMAB setup, base station antennas are treated as arms, and the environment state is defined by the current tilt configuration. The proposed DNN learns a policy for adjusting tilts based on contextual inputs, such as downlink channel state information (CSI) and user locations. By leveraging the DNN's ability to generalize, the system can adapt to new scenarios without requiring additional training. The effectiveness of this framework is validated through simulations demonstrating a significant increase in system throughput.

The article examines how lay individuals assess market exchanges involving their personal data and the emerging markets for human genetic information, utilizing findings from two distinct studies. The first study, a survey of 1,000 participants regarding personal data transactions, revealed that respondents frequently rejected the premise of a standard market framework. The second study, a qualitative analysis involving 20 interviews with participants about genetic data, uncovered a more nuanced picture that highlighted the limitations of relying solely on economic models to comprehend the social and ethical dimensions of such exchanges. Collectively, these findings suggest that current paradigms fail to adequately capture the complexities of these transactions.

This study introduces a Deep Learning (DL) framework designed to mitigate the computational complexity associated with detecting Flash-Orthogonal-Time-Nyquist (FTN) signaling. The FTN signaling approach enhances spectral efficiency by intentionally inducing controlled intersymbol interference (ISI). However, decoding FTN signals is notoriously difficult, necessitating high-complexity equalization and precise channel estimation. To address this, we propose a DL-driven receiver that utilizes a neural network to estimate the transmitted symbols directly from the distorted, received signals. This method bypasses the need for explicit equalization and channel estimation, thereby significantly lowering detection complexity. We evaluate the method's efficacy using FTN QPSK modulation, demonstrating that the DL receiver achieves performance comparable to a Maximum Likelihood (ML) detector. Furthermore, we illustrate that this deep learning architecture can be effectively adapted to support multiple modulation schemes.

We demonstrate that for any complete atomic distributive lattice, these two topologies coincide when applied to effect effect algebras. Furthermore, we establish that the underlying effect algebra of a complete effect algebra of $[0,1]$-valued measurable functions is precisely that of a complete effect algebra of $[0,1]$-valued measurable functions. This study introduces SaliencyMix, a novel data augmentation technique designed to enhance the robustness of object detection models. The approach leverages a saliency map to highlight regions within an image that are critical for a specific object detection model. Subsequently, it applies Mixup to blend these highlighted areas with corresponding regions from another image. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results on the MS COCO dataset, surpassing the performance of existing object detection models.

In 1988, Vershik and Kerov achieved a full classification of indecomposable positive traces on the infinite series Iwahiri--Hecke algebra, denoted $\mathcal{H}_n$, by establishing that every such trace decomposes uniquely into a linear combination of symmetric group algebra components $s_\lambda$ indexed by partitions. This note extends that result to the affine Hecke algebra $\mathcal{H}_n(q,t)$, which is generated by $n$ elements $s_i$ satisfying the braid relations and two additional generators $x_0$ and $x_1$ obeying specific commutation and quadratic rules. We demonstrate that indecomposable positive traces on $\mathcal{H}_n(q,t)$ are precisely the linear combinations of $s_\lambda$ where the coefficients are determined by the coefficients of a linear combination of indecomposable positive traces on $\mathcal{H}_n$.

This study introduces a novel method for analyzing the alignment between the quadrupole moments of dark matter haloes and the surrounding tidal field, utilizing the halo bispectrum. This approach enables the investigation of alignment mechanisms within modified gravity theories, such as the coupling between tidal fields and the intrinsic shapes of haloes. We demonstrate that the bispectrum serves as a robust statistical tool for quantifying alignment, offering a distinct advantage over the quadrupole-tidal correlation by effectively suppressing noise from random alignments. Furthermore, we examine the alignment of haloes in $f(R)$ gravity, a model characterized by a scale-dependent gravitational potential. Our findings indicate that the alignment strength in $f(R)$ gravity is significantly higher than in standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmology, with the magnitude of this effect directly proportional to the parameter governing the scale dependence of the potential. Consequently, we conclude that the halo bispectrum is a highly effective method for detecting both alignment phenomena and the scale-dependent nature of the gravitational potential inherent in modified gravity models.

Soft-deformable particle systems, such as networks of microtubules and actin, are ubiquitous in nature and are often modeled as viscoelastic materials. However, recent studies have revealed that these systems exhibit complex behaviors, including a history-dependent memory effect. This phenomenon is characterized by the observation that reversing strain after relaxing it for a specific duration yields a distinct response compared to immediate reversal. This research investigates the origins of such memory effects by applying a generalized Maxwell viscoelastic framework to simulate the cyclic loading and unloading of these systems. The findings demonstrate that these memory effects arise from the interplay between the system's viscoelastic properties and the specific boundary conditions applied. Furthermore, the study establishes that these systems possess a unique capability to "remember" their prior deformation history, which can be accessed and manipulated through subsequent deformation cycles.

This study examines the thermodynamic stability and phase transitions of gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) in aqueous environments using a coarse-grained model. By integrating a recently developed thermodynamic framework with a recently proposed phase-field approach, we simulate the formation of AuNPs in water and track their phase changes. Our results indicate that the thermodynamic stability of AuNPs is highly sensitive to particle size, with smaller particles exhibiting higher melting temperatures. Additionally, we observe that surface defects act as nucleation sites, facilitating phase transitions. These findings offer a theoretical basis for understanding the phase behavior of AuNPs in water and may guide the design of future experiments.

This study examines the impact of relaxing standard differentiability requirements on the assumptions concerning the nonlinear term within a quasi-linear elliptic boundary value problem. We demonstrate that this approach enables a more precise characterization of the solution space's regularity.

This study introduces a model featuring a $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry that resolves the anomalies associated with the SSM and $SU(3)_c$ by addressing the four horizontal anomalies through the correlation of quarks and anti-le leptons. The theory incorporates three right-handed neutrinos, which serve as dark matter candidates. Additionally, the model accounts for neutrino masses and mixing, predicts specific signatures for LHC searches, and outlines a viable framework for future neutrino experiments.

This study aims to establish identities for $(h; q)$-Genocchi numbers and polynomials by utilizing generating functions and the Fermion $q-$differential operator. We begin with the derivation of two identities rooted in the addition theorem for $m$-tuples of these numbers and polynomials. Subsequently, leveraging the Fermion $q-$differential operator, we derive identities for $m$-tuples of $(h; q)$-Genocchi polynomials. Furthermore, we establish relations concerning the $m$-tuples of $(h; q)$-Genocchi numbers through an application of the Cauchy-Hadamard theorem.

This study introduces a reinforcement learning framework for addressing nonstationary problems, aiming to estimate average rewards within an infinite-horizon setting. We propose an algorithm that adaptively balances exploration and exploitation by integrating a confidence interval for average-reward Q-learning with an upper confidence bound strategy. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the resulting regret is sublinear, and the method achieves consistency under mild assumptions. Furthermore, we validate our approach through numerical experiments on both synthetic data and real-world datasets.

Causal effect estimation is a primary goal in observational study analysis, yet it is typically hindered by confounding factors. While numerous methods exist to estimate the causal odds ratio (COR) under the assumption of unmeasured confounding, this paper introduces a novel approach that utilizes a specific type of known prior information. This information takes the form of the true COR observed in a specific subgroup of the study population. The proposed method, named the True Subgroup Odds Ratio (TSOR) estimator, leverages the known subgroup COR to adjust the overall estimate. We demonstrate that the TSOR estimator is unbiased and consistent, and we evaluate its performance through simulations. Additionally, the method is applied to real-world data from a cohort study investigating the association between antidepressant use and suicide attempts.

Autoencoders are widely employed for unsupervised learning, particularly in the form of deep generative models. These models are increasingly utilized for various tasks, including image generation, data compression, and dimensionality reduction. This study introduces a novel autoencoder architecture grounded in invertible layers, designed to enhance performance metrics such as log-likelihood and sample quality. The proposed invertible layers are built using the inverse of ReLU, a non-differentiable function, which is approximated via a piecewise linear strategy. This approximation technique is both straightforward to implement and computationally efficient. The proposed architecture is evaluated against existing invertible autoencoders, demonstrating superior performance. Additionally, the method is applied to the task of unsupervised image segmentation.

This study introduces optimal multigrid-based geometric multigrid preconditioners designed for hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin (HdG) linear systems. These methods are developed for both Cartesian and non-Cartesian grids, utilizing a novel approach to transfer and interpolate between grid levels that leverages the underlying geometry. The approach employs a coarse mesh of reduced resolution to approximate solutions, with the solution transfer performed by solving a local, sparse linear system on the fine mesh. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the preconditioned iterative solver's convergence rate remains independent of the Hdg polynomial degree $p$. Numerical experiments further validate the preconditioners' effectiveness and efficiency, confirming their performance across fine and coarse grids as well as on both Cartesian and non-Cartesian geometries.

This paper introduces a new approach to the E-value, extending its utility to scenarios involving data with missingness. By adapting the concept, we can quantify sensitivity to unobserved missing values and thereby measure the robustness of causal inferences. The method demonstrates that the E-value serves as a tool for assessing whether findings hold up under unmeasured confounding driven by missing data. We illustrate the application of this extended E-value using a study on the link between alcohol consumption and dementia, which faced substantial attrition among drinkers with established conditions. Additionally, we examine how a missing-data-based E-value interacts with traditional E-values for confounding, as well as its alignment with existing robustness assessments for missing data.

In crossover trials with few participants, missing data poses a significant challenge. This study examines the impact of a single missing value in a 2x2 crossover design through both simulation and analytical methods. We compared the performance of the standard analysis (last observation carried forward) against the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and a nonparametric bootstrap approach. Additionally, we utilized the bootstrap method to generate point estimates and confidence intervals for the average bioequivalence difference via a one-period sequence design. The analysis included a simulation of a 2x2 crossover with a one-period sequence design involving 10 participants, where data were missing from the second period for just one subject. The results indicate that the nonparametric bootstrap approach offers superior performance compared to the other methods evaluated.

This paper introduces a novel DRAM Physical Unclonable Function (PUF) that leverages the inherent variability of DRAM cells. The system employs a challenge-response mechanism where the PUF core consists of a DRAM array, and the challenge is defined by a specific set of read/write operations targeting individual cells. The resulting output is the collection of read values extracted from these locations. The proposed DRAM PUF is engineered to be resilient against challenges involving adversarial noise, replay attacks, and timing-based side-channel intrusions. The authors present a comprehensive evaluation of their implementation, covering various metrics such as robustness, entropy, and operational speed. The results demonstrate that this new DRAM PUF achieves comparable performance to current state-of-the-art solutions in terms of robustness and throughput, while offering significantly enhanced ease of integration.

This paper presents a novel framework for orchestrating and managing virtualized network functions, designed to align with functional programming paradigms. By leveraging the inherent capabilities of functional programming, this framework offers a declarative approach to network management that ensures robustness and reliability. The system is built upon the Python programming language and utilizes the Kubernetes container orchestration platform.

Toric code implementations offer a robust framework for evaluating the performance of quantum gates, as they are defined by a concise set of local operations. This study introduces a streamlined, single-qubit approach for simating toric code dynamics, which serves as a highly efficient alternative to traditional two-qubit architectures. We demonstrate that this reduced model accurately replicates key benchmarking metrics, including the growth of logical error rates and the impact of various noise models on gate fidelity. Furthermore, we identify that applying a specific noise model to the single-qubit system yields a benchmarking curve for Clifford gates that closely matches experimental data obtained from two-qubit systems. These findings suggest that the single-qubit simulation method is viable for practical use, potentially enabling real-time monitoring of quantum hardware performance.

The Universal Worker System (UWS) is a lightweight, adaptable framework designed to run jobs within a computing cluster. It operates as a service accessible via HTTP, allowing clients to submit tasks and monitor their status. Designed for flexibility, UWS can operate on dedicated worker nodes or be shared across multiple jobs within the same cluster. Additionally, it integrates with the Apache web server, enabling job submission through standard web browsers.

This study introduces a framework for "learning" across wireless communications, networking, and information theory, with a specific focus on leveraging machine learning and blockchain. Blockchain is utilized to ensure the integrity of data and models within a decentralized learning environment, while a multi-agent model-based deep reinforcement learning approach is developed to optimize the wireless network. This proposed method is benchmarked against a deep learning approach, demonstrating superior performance in scenarios where training data is limited.

The detection of oxygen (O2) and ozone (O3) in terrestrial exoplanet atmospheres is often considered a potential biosphere indicator. However, recent findings suggest that these species can accumulate in the atmospheres of sterile planets, complicating the interpretation of their presence. This study investigates how host star temperature influences the O2-O3 relationship and ozone generation in Earth-like exoplanets. We employed a 1D radiative-convective model to simulate atmospheres of rocky planets orbiting M, K, and G-type stars, subject to varying levels of stellar XUV radiation and different atmospheric compositions. Our results indicate that for planets with high CO2 levels, O3 production is minimal, and O2-O3 correlations remain weak. Conversely, in atmospheres dominated by N2, O3 production is significantly higher, and O2-O3 correlations are strong. Furthermore, we observe that O3 production rates are markedly higher in planets orbiting cooler stars compared to those orbiting hotter stars. These findings suggest that O3 production is more robust in N2-dominated atmospheres and that O3 production is more efficient in planets orbiting cooler stars.

This study examines the resilience of surface currents within the framework of the surface Haldane model. We demonstrate that surface currents remain robust against disorder in both bosonic and fermionic systems. For the fermionic scenario, this robustness is attributed to the topological protection inherent in the bulk. In contrast, the bosonic system exhibits disorder-free surface currents even in the absence of topological protection, a phenomenon we attribute to a specific symmetry of the effective Hamiltonian. Furthermore, we establish that surface currents are sensitive to the breaking of either fermionic or bosonic symmetries, a finding that offers a viable method for controlling topological surface currents in the Bose-Hubbard model.

This paper introduces a multilingual neural machine translation (M-MT) model designed to leverage data from various domains, specifically targeting medical applications. The approach utilizes a domain-adaptive MMT model that integrates a pre-trained BERT encoder with a Transformer decoder, trained on a corpus combining both in-domain and out-of-domain data. The study evaluates the performance of this domain-adaptive model against both in-domain-only and out-of-domain-only baselines using the WMT-2016 multilingual test set and an out-of-domain medical test set. The results indicate that the domain-adaptive model outperforms the out-of-domain model on the medical evaluation set, achieving a BLEU score increase of 1.7. Additionally, it surpasses the out-of-domain baseline on the WMT-2016 multilingual test set by a BLEU margin of 1.3.

This study examines the generation of both solitary and shock structures within a magnetized, electron-rich, and non-Maxwellian plasma environment. Utilizing the reductive perturbation technique, we derived the non-linear non-local form of the Korteweg-de Vries-Zakharov-Kulzhov (NKZK) equation to analyze these phenomena. The analysis reveals that the NKZK equation accurately models the observed phenomena, with the findings indicating that the ion fluid temperature and electron non-thermal parameter are critical factors in determining whether solitary or shock waves form. Additionally, an analytical solution for the amplitude of the resulting nonlinear waves was obtained. The theoretical results are substantiated by numerical simulations, which further highlight the influence of the plasma's non-Maxwellian characteristics on the amplitude of nonlinear waves.

We introduce a new multilingual sentence representation learning approach that utilizes contrastive context prediction (CCP) and a multilingual masked language model (MLM) pre-trained on extensive corpora. Our method trains the CCP task using the multilingual MLM, leveraging its ability to predict masked tokens to generate context representations. By framing the CCP task as a contrastive learning problem, we achieve state-of-the-art results on the CLUE benchmark, surpassing existing methods. Additionally, we demonstrate that the proposed representations are effective for few-shot and zero-shot learning scenarios.

This study introduces a multimodal learning framework designed to mitigate the performance gap between fast and slow modalities. The core of our approach, termed Prototypical Modality Rebalance (PMR), involves deriving prototypical representations for each class within every modality. By leveraging these prototypes, the framework generates modality-specific targets to recalibrate the learning process, enabling slower modalities to more effectively emulate the features of faster ones. The resulting target serves as a joint objective for balancing the contribution of all modalities. Empirical evaluations across various benchmarks, including ImageNet, MS-COCO, and AIST, demonstrate that our method significantly enhances the performance of slow modalities while maintaining parity with fast ones. Furthermore, the approach exhibits robustness against modality imbalance and domain shifts. The implementation is accessible at https://github.com/ruixu1996/PMR.

We examine kinetic equations for massless fermions within a conformally invariant background, accounting for the non-cancellation of the local particle number density's divergence by the time derivative of the scale factor. This divergence stems from the time-dependence of the scale factor and necessitates a correction to the standard kinetic equations for such systems.

This study introduces a cascaded model combining a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) with a Deep Neural Network (DNN) to address the issue of parameter inefficiency in traditional CNNs. The approach involves using a lightweight, pre-trained small CNN to extract features from raw audio, which are then passed to a larger, more powerful DNN for command recognition. This hybrid architecture, designated as CNN+(TT-DNN), significantly boosts the accuracy of the standalone DNN while maintaining a 100-fold reduction in the total number of parameters compared to using a full-sized DNN alone. Experiments conducted on the wake-word challenge dataset confirm that the proposed model achieves a 96.7% accuracy rate, surpassing the 90.7% accuracy of a traditional DNN with an equally small parameter count.

This study examines the dynamics of a two-level system driven by a time-dependent, off-resonant laser field, which is coupled to an external environment. The interaction is modeled using a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian that incorporates the laser's complex Rabi frequency. We demonstrate that by adjusting the laser's Rabi frequency and detuning, the system's time evolution can be precisely controlled to align with a specific target state. Furthermore, we provide a method to determine the necessary Rabi frequency and detuning values for achieving this controlled evolution.

We present a plasmonic solar cell utilizing an aluminum film that supports localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) within the visible spectrum. This device converts incident light into electrical current with a peak photon-to-electron conversion efficiency of 14.4% at a wavelength of 550 nm. This high efficiency is achieved by integrating an ultrathin aluminum film with a silicon substrate, leveraging the aluminum film's ability to absorb light and generate hot carriers. By adjusting the aluminum film's thickness, we can precisely tune the LSPR frequency, thereby optimizing the conversion efficiency for specific wavelengths.

This study introduces an algebra of binary relations that integrates linear-time modal dynamic $\mu$-logic, specifically tailored to capture the linear computational processes inherent in $\mu$-calculus models. The proposed framework extends prior algebraic methods for branching-time $\mu$-calculus by incorporating the linear order of relations. This extension facilitates a straightforward examination of the $\mu$-calculus's linear fragments, yielding a new characterization of linear fragments within the linear fragment of the $\mu$-calculus.

This study introduces a novel Federated Deep Learning (FED) framework built upon a custom hardware accelerator, the FDHT-LSTM, which integrates Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) and Hartley Transform (HHT) techniques with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) units. Designed to address the computational intensity of LSTM operations, this architecture leverages tensor decomposition to significantly lower memory access costs. The FDHT-LSTM is specifically engineered for the FED-LSTM model, which utilizes LSTM networks to train deep neural networks (DNNs) within federated environments. Experimental results indicate that the FDHT-LSTM outperforms conventional tensor-decomposed, model-centric hardware designs in both throughput and energy efficiency. Furthermore, the FED-LSTM model, when deployed on this optimized hardware, surpasses standard federated DNN approaches in terms of convergence speed, overall accuracy, and communication efficiency.

UAVs and unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) are increasingly utilized in civilian sectors, including agriculture, where they are often controlled via wireless links. These communications must be secured against eavesdropping and spoofing to ensure safety and reliability. While the MAVLink protocol is designed to be language-agnostic, the lack of standardized security implementations has led to inconsistent security measures across different systems. This study evaluates the efficiency of various encryption algorithms within the context of MAVLink communications. The research focuses on the computational overhead and the resulting impact on the total flight time of UAVs. The findings indicate that AES is the most efficient choice for securing these messages, whereas RSA is the least efficient.

This paper introduces a novel methodology for deriving network emulation models by analyzing the impact of architectural changes on end-to-end characteristics. The approach is applied to a specific case: a data-centric, wireless, mobile IP network. The findings demonstrate that shifts in network structure do not always alter end-to-end properties, enabling the use of simplified, equivalent models for analysis. Furthermore, these emergend-to-end properties facilitate the development of novel emulation frameworks. The study concludes with a discussion on the broader implications of these results for future research.

We demonstrate that the Newman-Penrose mapping admits a completely equivalent twistor representation. While the original formulation remains geometrically invariant, the original formulation maintains a full geometrically invariant, an equivalent twistor representation loses this invariance.

Cosmic ray muon telescopes are increasingly utilized across diverse fields, including archaeology, geology, and civil engineering. This study introduces a compact, low-cost, and highly sensitive muon telescope designed for detecting artifacts within the Egyptian pyramids. The device features a 128-channel silicon photomultiplier (SiPM)-based scintillation array, with each channel measuring 10 mm in diameter and 10 cm in length. The SiPMs are housed in a vacuum-sealed, hermetically sealed enclosure to ensure operational stability. The system's energy resolution was evaluated using a 90 kBq ⁵⁵Cr source, yielding an average of 1.5 photoelectrons per detected muon. This signal allows for the discrimination of low-energy background noise, such as that from ⁵⁵Cr and ⁴⁰K, from actual cosmic ray muon events. The telescope's performance was validated through simulations and tests involving a ⁵⁵Cr source, with the resulting energy resolution matching the simulation predictions.

This work introduces PEGLL, a novel parsing algorithm that extends the Earley-Gleason-Larson (GLL) approach to support context-free languages defined by arbitrary deterministic pushdown automata. While standard GLL methods are limited to specific subclasses of grammars, the proposed algorithm is capable of handling a broader spectrum of grammar types. We demonstrate the soundness and completeness of PEGLL, and present a refined version of the algorithm that reduces its space requirements to linear complexity.

This study examines the spontaneous and stimulated emission of photons by a neutral scalar particle in a thermal bath. We demonstrate that the process remains unitary, as the sum of the probability for transitions to final states and the probability of inverse transitions equals unity. Photon emission rates are derived using the Källén-Lehmann spectral representation, which incorporates thermal modifications to the photon propagator.

This study examines how linguistic context influences the neural processing of predicted and unpredic ted words. We introduce a novel word predictability metric that incorporates extended linguistic contexts, arguing that prior context is essential for accurately modeling surprise responses during language comprehension. Our experiments utilized a multilingual BERT model, fine-tuned on the Penn Treebank corpus, to simulate human cognitive processing. We found that our approach to measuring predictability aligns better with human behavioral data than do existing methods. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that linguistic context significantly affects word predictability, with prior context substantially reducing the neural divergence between predicted and unpredic ted words.

This paper introduces a novel 3D object estimation framework designed to learn canonical poses from unlabeled data. Our approach utilizes a multi-stage training scheme that progressively refines the learning of these poses. Initially, a 2D detector is trained to identify 2D object instances, which are then projected into 3D space to generate pose estimates. Subsequently, a neural network is trained to predict 6D poses from these projections. To further enhance the quality of the 3D pose estimates, we implement a refinement stage that fine-tunes the network using the previously generated pose estimates as supervision. This method is demonstrated on the 3D object detection task, where it achieves state-of-the-art results on the 3DObjectDetectors dataset.

We investigate the intrinsic spin-orbit coupling in indium antimonide (InSb) nanowires, examining how it influences the coupling between quantum dots separated by a tunnel barrier. Our analysis reveals that the spin-orbit interaction can be utilized to modulate tunneling rates by applying an external magnetic field. Additionally, we explore the feasibility of a spin-filtration device where the spin-dependent transmission probabilities for electrons with opposite spins differ by several orders of magnitude.

This study introduces a novel 2D simulation framework for radiation belt particle dynamics that incorporates pitch-angle scattering, a critical feature absent in standard 2D models. By employing a Fokker-Planck equation, the framework accounts for this scattering process, which is essential for accurately describing particle behavior during geomagnetic storms. The analysis reveals that incorporating this mechanism significantly alters particle energy distributions, with the magnitude of change depending on the specific energy levels and the scattering rate. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that the new 2D model yields results consistent with 3D simulations, thereby validating its effectiveness. These findings underscore the necessity of including pitch-angle scattering in 2D modeling approaches to ensure realistic representations of radiation belt dynamics.

The precision measurement of the Higgs diphoton decay rate offers a potent means to investigate the Higgsstrahlung process. This approach is particularly effective for probing extended scalar sectors, as it can reveal new particles that couple to the Higgs field. We demonstrate that the combination of Higgsstrahlung and the diphoton channel surpasses the sensitivity of direct searches for heavy vector bosons. Furthermore, we establish that the diphoton-Higgsstrahlung correlation can be utilized to constrain the parameter space of non-Abelian gauge theories featuring a Higgsstrahlung process.

This study examines the application of differential privacy (DP) in financial machine learning, specifically focusing on two DP implementations: DP-SGD and PATE. We evaluate their performance using a real-world dataset of credit card transactions, analyzing the relationship between privacy loss and model accuracy. Our findings indicate that, for this specific task, PATE delivers superior results compared to DP-SGD. Furthermore, we demonstrate that utilizing a pre-trained model significantly enhances the efficacy of the PATE framework.

This work extends the general Wold decomposition framework established by Hildebrandt and Taqqu (2010) to cover multivariate second-order random distribution fields. The proposed version of this decomposition is further utilized to examine the behavior of the fractional Gaussian field in multiple dimensions.

This study examines the impact of dust and impurities on the ignition of a gas mixture using a laser. The analysis utilizes a two-dimensional computational model to simulate the interaction between a laser beam and a combustible gas. The results indicate that the presence of dust and impurities significantly alters the ignition characteristics of the mixture.

This paper introduces the Boundary-Aware Segmentation Network (BANS), a new approach for image segmentation that leverages a multi-scale encoder-decoder framework. The architecture employs a U-Net backbone, enhanced by a dedicated boundary module that integrates both the original input and a Laplacian pyramid to generate precise segmentation masks. This module specifically targets edge refinement to ensure high-quality results. The BANS model was trained and evaluated on the Cityscapes dataset, demonstrating superior performance against existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we developed two practical applications based on this framework: a real-time segmentation system for autonomous driving and a mobile application designed for medical image segmentation.

This paper introduces the Driver-Messenger System (DMS), a cooperative framework designed to facilitate safe lane changes by distributing tasks between the road vehicle and autonomous agents. The vehicle focuses on navigation and steering, while the agents execute lateral movements. The study examines a scenario involving a driver and a group of agents positioned in a single lane, where the driver must enter a target lane and agents must reach a destination lane. The authors analyze the computational complexity of the problem, demonstrating that determining an optimal solution is NP-hard. To address this, they propose a heuristic approach that generates a sequence of scenarios, each solvable in polynomial time, to produce a feasible solution. The paper further evaluates the method's performance through simulations, comparing it against baseline strategies.

This study examines the local density distribution of active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particles interacting with various geometric boundaries. By utilizing the thermodynamic limit of large particle numbers, we derive a closed-form equation for the density profile. This approach yields an exact analytical solution for planar boundaries and provides a general formula applicable to arbitrary curvilinear boundaries. The results demonstrate that active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particles accumulate near boundaries, with the magnitude of this accumulation increasing as the boundary curvature decreases. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model and the Run and Tumble (RT) model, showing that both frameworks can be unified within the framework of generalized Fokker-Planck equations.

The paper introduces the application of Siegert states to electronic structure calculations within a plasma environment, utilizing the average atom model. In this framework, average atom Siegert states are constructed by solving the plasma-specific Kohn-Sham equation, employing a complex, real-space-based plasma model that accounts for electron screening and incorporates the plasma's complex dielectric function. These calculations are performed using the open-source finite-difference code FDMES. The resulting average atom Siegert states are then used to compute plasma absorption and emission spectra. The approach is validated against existing literature and demonstrates strong agreement. Furthermore, the method is applied to determine spectra for sodium and argon, with results compared to experimental data and other theoretical models, confirming its effectiveness.

This study examines the Si IV 10926 Å line in the quiet Sun and during a flare using the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS) on the Sun. We analyzed the Doppler shifts of the Si IV 10926 Å line's secondary component, which is associated with plasma flows in the upper transition region. In the quiet Sun, this component typically exhibits a blueshift of approximately -10 km s$^{-1}$, a value that aligns with prior research. During the flare, however, the redshift of this component increases significantly, reaching up to 100 km s$^{-1}$. This shift correlates with the upward movement of the flare's coronal loop footpoints, which are visible in the H$\alpha$ 6563 Å line. We propose that the substantial blueshifts observed in the Si IV 10926 Å line's secondary component during flares result from the upward acceleration of the lower transition region plasma.

This study examines the quantum chromodynamics (QCD) framework within the context of a universe featuring a non-zero, non-antimatter-cancelling theta parameter ($\theta \neq 0$). We demonstrate that this specific configuration offers a solution to the strong CP anomaly, proposing that the cosmos operates with a non-zero electric theta value ($\theta_{\rm ED}$). Furthermore, we establish that this state is dynamically stable, suggesting that such a universe could have emerged spontaneously during the earliest moments of the Big Bang.

Amorphous thin films subjected to ion irradiation exhibit an interface that migrates at a constant rate, with its velocity direction always normal to itself. This interface behavior can be derived geometrically by considering the intersection of two distinct, independent, and non-interacting surfaces: the irradiation isosurface and a virtual surface known as the "irradiation isosurface" (or more precisely, the "irradiation isosurface" is a conceptual construct). The irradiation isosurface is defined by the locus of points where the cumulative irradiation dose equals a specific threshold. The motion of the interface is governed by the intersection of these two surfaces.

This article introduces a novel software design pattern, "Router," which enables the protection of source code against plagiarism. The approach involves a system that allows users to input source code and then retrieves the code's "fingerprint"—a unique representation that can be indexed in a search database. The Router's implementation is straightforward, utilizing the code's syntax tree as input and generating the fingerprint as output. The core methodology employs a probabilistic algorithm that iterates through the syntax tree, assigning a probability to each node. The final fingerprint consists of the set of nodes with a probability greater than 0.5. The paper provides a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the algorithm, including a demonstration of its correctness and an examination of its time complexity.

We establish that for the class $\mathcal{Z}$, the lower bound for the abscissa of absolute convergence is $1/2$, matching the classical limit found in the Riemann zeta function. This result is achieved by leveraging the connection between $\mathcal{Z}$ and the Riemann zeta function, combined with an analysis of the asymptotic behavior of its elements.

We demonstrate that if a group possesses bounded exponent, any $(k,r)$-metric approximate subgroup can be expanded into a $(k')r^{O_1(1)}$-approximate subgroup. This finding establishes a direct link between the metric and algebraic approaches to the Approximate Groups Conjecture.

We introduce novel algorithms for efficiently calculating log-concave maximum likelihood estimators. By leveraging randomized and Nesterov-type smoothing techniques, these methods achieve computational speeds that surpass existing state-of-the-art approaches. The new algorithms are straightforward to implement, easy to use, and have been made available as an R package named `logcon`. Additionally, we propose a robust variant of these estimators that is less sensitive to outliers, with corresponding code also provided as an R package.

The non-interacting rigid arch model, which accounts for the topological arrangement of force chains, has been established as a highly effective method for predicting the stability of granular systems. This study investigates how the model's validity extends to granular assemblies with a broad range of friction coefficients, $\mu$. We demonstrate that the model remains applicable for systems with $\mu \leq 1.5$, provided that the dimensionless friction coefficient is rescaled by the arch formation probability, $P_{\rm arch}$. Furthermore, we show that the relationship between $P_{\rm arch}$ and $\mu$ is universal across various packing densities and particle size distributions.

This paper examines a game played on directed graphs where two players alternately move a token along edges, with the objective for both sides being to determine the shortest path length to traverse a specified set of vertices. While the game is NP-hard for general directed graphs, we establish polynomial-time solvability for specific instances, such as those with a fixed number of target nodes, and provide hardness proofs for other structural categories.

The spectral density of stochastic processes is a valuable tool for characterizing random motion, as it can differentiate between processes such as Brownian motion and superdiffusive behaviors. This study introduces a method to determine the spectral density of fractional Brownian motion (fBm) using the Hurst exponent, a parameter that defines fBm's long-range correlations. By applying this approach to the velocity of a self-propelled particle, we successfully identified the transition from diffusive to superdiffusive dynamics. Our findings demonstrate that the spectral density of the velocity effectively captures the anomalous diffusion exponent, which is a key indicator of the particle's motion type.

This study examines the higher-order Broer-Kaup (HBK) system, a variant of the classical Broer-Kaup (BK) system, which is known for modeling shallow water waves. The BK system is notable for possessing a Lax pair and integrability, whereas the higher-order variant is not yet established as integrable. The primary objective of this work is to demonstrate the integrability of the HBK system by constructing a Lax pair and utilizing the inverse scattering transform (IST) method. The analysis begins with the derivation of the HBK system's bilinear form, followed by the construction of a Lax pair. Subsequently, the paper establishes the direct scattering problem and the associated inverse problem. The solvability of the HBK system is then proven through the IST framework, and finally, the paper derives the explicit 1-soliton solutions for this system.

This paper introduces VIRUP, a software package designed for creating and rendering virtual environments. Built upon the open-source Blender 3D suite, VIRUP offers a Python API enabling users to develop custom scripts that define scene pre-selection and render sequences. Additionally, the software supports scripting for the automated generation of scenes, including mesh and texture creation, and the scheduling of rendering tasks.

Data-Paths in Software-Defined Networking (SDN) are typically defined through abstract specifications, yet verifying that the deployed paths align with these specifications is crucial for security and correctness. This paper introduces a straightforward, scalable method for verifying that the abstract paths specified by SDN controllers are correctly implemented in OpenFlow switches. The approach involves constructing a finite-state model of the network, utilizing a formal specification language to describe the intended path, and subsequently verifying the model against this specification. This verification process is achieved through automated model checking. The methodology is demonstrated in a case study where the paper presents a novel tool, OpenModelChecker, designed to facilitate the verification of OpenFlow switches.

Generative models are frequently employed to create novel data by adjusting latent codes, yet this process relies on disentanglement, which is often difficult to achieve. This study proposes a new method to facilitate controlled latent code modifications by establishing weak disentanglement. We introduce a training objective that encourages the model to learn a low-dimensional manifold where specific dimensions govern distinct features. This approach allows for targeted alterations to latent codes, enabling the synthesis of new samples with desired attributes. Experiments across various datasets demonstrate that this objective effectively learns a low-dimensional representation, and the resulting manifold proves beneficial for both image translation and super-resolution tasks.

This study examines the aerodynamic efficiency of a two-dimensional, two-foil configuration using a leading and trailing element. The analysis focuses on a specific kinematic pattern where both foils oscillate sinusoidally with identical frequencies and phase offsets, operating within a Reynolds number range of $10^4$ to $10^5$. Through a combination of numerical simulations and physical experiments, the research investigates how varying parameters—including foil spacing, oscillation amplitudes, and phase shifts—affect the flow dynamics and overall efficiency. The findings indicate that the trailing foil's performance is primarily driven by the strength of the leading edge vortices (LEVs) and the characteristics of the vortex shedding from the leading foil. Specifically, the trailing foil achieves peak efficiency when it remains in phase with the LEVs generated by the leading foil. Furthermore, the study reveals that the maximum attainable efficiency in this coupled configuration exceeds that of isolated foils, with the highest efficiency levels occurring at a specific combination of foil spacing, oscillation amplitudes, and phase shift.

Determining the spectral function is a fundamental challenge in real-time physics, yet existing methods struggle with ill-posedness. We introduce a new technique that utilizes a neural network to learn the mapping from spectral functions to their Fourier transforms, subsequently applying the inverse Fourier transform to recover the original spectral function. This approach is demonstrated on gluon spectral functions derived from quantum chromodynamics at finite temperature, yielding results that align well with perturbative calculations.

A quantum dot can serve as a probe to determine the energy gap and spectral features of a superconductor when connected via a Josephson tunneling process. This study examines the stability of the resulting supercurrent across the entire range of Josephson phases. We find that the current-voltage characteristics of the system are influenced by the superconductor's spectral properties, which are reflected in the phase dependence of the quasiparticle tunneling rate. Our analysis demonstrates that the tunneling rate can be expressed as a Fourier series of the superphase, with coefficients determined by the addition spectrum. Consequently, the current's Fourier components can be utilized to extract these spectral coefficients. This approach is particularly effective for identifying subgap structures in the addition spectrum, offering a method to study the quasiparticle spectrum of superconductors with high precision.

The quest for new therapeutic solutions has been a cornerstone of scientific advancement for centuries, yet the traditional drug discovery process remains costly and time-consuming. To address these challenges, researchers have increasingly turned to computational methods to accelerate drug development. This study introduces a generative approach designed to create novel drug molecules by leveraging the physicochemical properties of existing ones. We employ a deep learning framework that utilizes convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to model the probability distributions of drug molecule properties. This framework is capable of generating new molecules that adhere to specific target property profiles. Furthermore, we validate the efficacy of this generative model by synthesizing a new class of compounds with tunable properties, specifically aimed at inhibiting the enzyme *E. coli* DNA gyrase.

This paper presents the Dynamic GoI Machine (DGoIM), a fresh abstract machine built upon Goard and Jouannaud's GoI Machine. We demonstrate that the DGoIM adheres to the classification scheme for abstract machines established by Accattali. Specifically, the DGoIM falls within the category of "the third generation." Our proof relies on the observation that the DGoIM aligns with the third generation abstract machine known as the DGoJ, which was developed by Hamano, GoJ, and Iwama.

This study introduces a machine learning approach for analyzing stellar populations in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) by utilizing data from the Gaia-ESO Survey (GES). The authors developed a random forest classifier to categorize LMC stars into three groups: thin-disk, thick-disk, and halo. The training dataset comprised 1,000 GES stars with known kinematics and chemical abundances, while the test set consisted of 1,000 LMC stars identified via photometry. The resulting model achieved an accuracy of 90.5% on the test set. Furthermore, the study examines the model's ability to distinguish between thick-disk and halo populations, analyzes the sources of misclassification, and evaluates the method's generalizability.

This study introduces a novel approach to identifying electricity theft by leveraging the time-series characteristics of consumption data. The proposed method utilizes a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to forecast load consumption, subsequently feeding these predictions into a Random Forest classifier to detect anomalies. The framework is evaluated using the public dataset from the KDD 2016 Data Mining Cup on Smart Metering. Results indicate that the proposed LSTM-based detection model outperforms existing state-of-the-art solutions, achieving a 99.99% F1-score.

This paper investigates sparse and tight graphs embedded on surfaces, specifically focusing on the torus. We identify 10 distinct base graphs that are irreducible, which serve as fundamental components for constructing these structures on the torus. Leveraging these bases, we have formulated a comprehensive set of generation rules that produce every possible irreducible graph. Additionally, we have developed and tested a software tool designed to generate and analyze both sparse and tight graphs defined over the torus.

This study reports the initial measurement of the $\Omega^0_c$ baryon lifetime, utilizing a data sample of $3.0\,\text{fb}^{-1}$ collected by the LHCb experiment at center-of-mass energies of $7$ and $8\,\text{TeV}$. The analysis focuses on the decay chain $\Xi_{cc}^+ \to \Omega^0_c K^+ \to \Lambda_c^+ K^- K^+ K^- K^-$. The resulting lifetime is determined to be $\tau_{\Omega^0_c} = (299.5 \pm 10.0 \pm 6.0)\,\text{fs}$, where the first uncertainty stems from statistical limitations and the second arises from systematic effects. This value aligns with prior measurements and yields a lower limit of $\tau_{\Omega^0_c} > 200\,\text{fs}$ at $90\%$ confidence level.

Sparse Subspace Clustering (SSC) is a prevalent unsupervised learning technique for segmenting data into clusters. Although existing SSC methods are effective, they suffer from high computational costs and fail to leverage spatial information within the affinity matrix. This paper introduces a novel algorithm that addresses these limitations by integrating a graph convolutional network (GCN) to extract features from the affinity matrix, thereby generating a refined clustering result. Our approach first constructs an affinity matrix to represent the data subspace, then applies graph convolutional layers to capture local and global features, and finally utilizes these features to produce an enhanced affinity matrix for clustering. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art SSC algorithms in clustering accuracy and computational efficiency.

This study introduces a new model for simulating the evolution of sea ice melt ponds, which are crucial for the ice energy balance. The model utilizes a stochastic framework to track the expansion and merging of individual ponds, generating a stochastic partial differential equation for the density of melt ponds as a function of size. We derive the associated forward equation and a weak solution, establishing the existence of a solution. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the density function exhibits a singularity at the critical size threshold, representing the point where merging ceases.

We demonstrate that the shift in final spin states during atom-molecule scattering can be mitigated by employing a Floquet framework. This approach attributes the suppression mechanism to destructive interference arising from the coupling of the scattering process with dressed states generated by a microwave field. This interference effect is quantified using the scattering matrix derived from the Floquet formalism. Furthermore, we propose a method to enhance this suppression mechanism by adjusting the microwave field's frequency and phase.

This study demonstrates the link between correlated anomalous diffusion and $q$-Gaussian distributions by utilizing a matrix-valued time-fractional Fokker-Planck equation. The resulting generalized $q$-Lévy process is derived as the corresponding stochastic model.

This paper introduces a reputation management protocol designed for the Decentralized Cloud Computing System (DCCS). Within this framework, the system is modeled as a Markov decision process (MDP) where reputation serves as the state variable. The study details the state transition dynamics and the calculation of the associated MDP model. The authors demonstrate that the problem can be effectively solved using a Markov chain. The paper further analyzes the long-term expected reward and the expected number of steps required to reach a specific target reputation level.

This study introduces a novel linear perceptual quality metric designed for point clouds. The approach begins by converting point clouds into vectorized representations, which are then processed through a 3D convolutional neural network (3D-CNN) to extract deep features. These features are utilized to train a linear perceptual model that demonstrates a correlation with subjective Mean Opinion Scores (MOS) exceeding 0.9, outperforming current state-of-the-art objective measures. Additionally, the model effectively correlates with MOS across various objective and subjective full-reference and no-reference quality metrics. The method's efficacy is further validated through its strong alignment with subjective MOS and NQMOS in full-reference scenarios as well as in no-reference scenarios.

We investigate the phase transition of black holes in a five-dimensional asymptotically anti-de Sitter black brane geometry, which serves as a holographic dual to quarkyonic transitions in QCD theory. Our analysis demonstrates that the bulk black hole phase transition corresponds to the quarkyonic transition within the dual theory. Furthermore, we establish that the first-order nature of this transition is contingent upon the QCD scale parameter, $\Lambda_{\text{QCD}}$.

This study introduces a novel, self-supervised deep learning framework designed to analyze knee MRI scans for anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) and medial collateral ligament (MCL) tears. The approach involves segmenting the ligaments and classifying the entire scan based on individual slice data. Specifically, the system employs a self-supervised model to generate semantic segmentation maps for the ACL and MCL, which are then used to isolate these structures on every MRI slice. Subsequently, the study evaluates the efficacy of a self-supervised learning model trained on these single slices for comprehensive knee MRI classification. Experimental results indicate that this slice-based method outperforms contemporary state-of-the-art techniques in classifying full knee MRI scans for ACL and MCL tears. Additionally, the segmentation module effectively delineates the complete anatomy of both ligaments across all slices. These findings suggest that this framework holds significant potential for developing advanced, self-supervised deep learning models for diagnosing knee injuries.

This paper introduces a new font generation method that creates stylistic variations of existing typefaces using a specific style code. Our approach employs cross-attention mechanisms to integrate the style code directly into content tokens, ensuring that learned character representations remain robust against minor input perturbations. Additionally, we integrate a style token into the latent space of the style encoder, enabling the system to capture the underlying structure of font landscapes. This design allows for the synthesis of fonts with diverse attributes and the execution of multi-point interpolation. Our method supports both novel font creation from scratch and the variation of existing fonts, with extensive experiments demonstrating superior performance and generalization capabilities.

This study examines the covariant formulation of the energy-momentum tensor for a charged fluid within the framework of Einstein's gravity augmented by a non-minimal torsion field. The torsion field is assumed to couple with the electromagnetic field, while the fluid's electric charge is also non-minimally coupled to this torsion field. The analysis demonstrates that the covariant structure of the energy-momentum tensor is altered by the fluid's interaction with the non-minimal torsion field. The paper further investigates the dynamical equations governing the charged fluid's motion and provides a comprehensive discussion of the resulting dynamical results.

Quality-of-Experience (QoE) optimization in video streaming is a critical challenge. While deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has proven effective in enhancing QoE, its application to video streaming is still emerging. This paper introduces an innovative DRL-based framework designed to maximize QoE by dynamically adjusting streaming parameters in real-time. The approach employs a deep neural network to learn the complex, non-linear relationship between QoE and various system variables. Furthermore, we developed a novel reward function that balances QoE improvements against network resource consumption. The proposed method was rigorously tested using the widely adopted Netflix QoE model, with performance evaluated through both simulation and real-world experiments. Results indicate that the DRL-driven approach significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving superior QoE outcomes with notably lower network costs.

This work examines the quintic nonlinear Schrödinger equation in two dimensions, $i\partial_t u + \Delta u = |u|^4u$, which is known to be analytically ill-posed in $L^1_t C_x^{t L^2}_x$. We establish that the equation is globally well-posed within $L^1_t C_x^{t L^2}_x$ spaces, provided the initial data are sufficiently small.

This study examines packet-level scheduling and coding across several links to optimize data transmission to a specific destination. The analysis encompasses both scenarios where packets are generated periodically and those generated on demand. For periodic generation, we introduce a new algorithm that leverages packet coding and scheduling capabilities to achieve a reduced total delivery delay. Conversely, for on-demand generation, we propose a protocol that adapts the packet generation rate based on whether data is available at the source, thereby balancing delay against throughput. Simulation results indicate that our proposed solutions outperform existing methods in both generation scenarios.
